contexts.context: The excerpt identifies a progression in SEM optimization from operator-controlled focus, stigmation, and beam alignment to automated algorithms and machine-learning systems. Early automated autofocus methods used image-sharpness metrics but were limited by noise and complex sample structures. Later work applied deep learning: a 2019 dual-network system used one network to evaluate focus quality and another to control working distance, while a 2021 method addressed defocus in secondary-electron SEM images. A 2024 approach used beam-profile deconvolution and kernel estimation to independently optimize focus, stigmator X/Y, and aperture alignment X/Y without requiring prior sample knowledge. The excerpt also notes reinforcement learning for real-time imaging-parameter optimization, hybrid ML/classical image-processing methods, GAN-generated SEM images, and ML-enabled closed-loop STEM operation. Its key distinction is between optimizing instrument settings after an operator has selected acquisition conditions and recommending acquisition parameters at a higher level from previously collected images, producing sample-specific guidelines intended to improve reproducibility and comparability. It therefore supports positioning an uncertainty-aware recommender as broader and more decision-oriented than autofocus or post-acquisition correction, but does not itself establish how such a system compares with Bayesian or autonomous microscopy literature.

It does, however, present an embedded-course model for involving students in meaningful open-science work. The authors recommend starting small by integrating one or two topics into existing MSc or PhD methods, programming, data-analysis, or soft-skills courses. Participation should count toward degree requirements rather than being treated as extracurricular, which helps establish open science as a normal academic working standard and supports student motivation. Projects should use scientifically meaningful data or research questions rather than “play projects.” In the authors’ example, students conducted open-science projects as partial fulfillment of a neurocognitive methods course, using data collected in their laboratories. Such projects can train essential analytical and reproducibility skills while enabling students to critically re-evaluate previously analyzed data and potentially improve the scientific record. Implementation is aided by identifying sympathetic faculty, supportive supervisors, departmental infrastructure, and sufficient time. The reported evaluation was promising but preliminary, based on a small, field-specific sample, so the excerpt does not establish a broadly validated model. These principles could inform trainee participation in community curation by embedding curation tasks in credited, scientifically consequential coursework and mentorship.

It does, however, provide criteria relevant to comparing such tools. Microscopy data systems should capture reproducible microscope conditions—including accelerating voltage, magnification, camera length, defocus, beam current, detector information, environmental conditions, sample preparation, and calibration records—along with technical image metadata such as file type, imager information, gain settings, and pixel size. They also emphasize persistent identifiers, links to samples, instruments, notebooks, and other data sources, controlled vocabularies, standardized units, and automated metadata collection. contexts.context: The excerpt provides useful context for comparing microscopy data standards, but it does not discuss kikuchipy, EMsoft, or OME-Zarr, nor does it evaluate parameter recommendation capabilities. OME is described as an open-source framework supporting exchange and analysis of primarily biological microscopy images. OME-XML supplies structured metadata for acquisition parameters, instrument settings, and sample details, with standardized optical-component names such as Filter, Objective, and Laser. Its principal limitation for materials microscopy is its predominant orientation toward optical biology applications. NeXus is an open scientific-data storage and exchange format used in neutron, x-ray, and muon experiments. NXem extends it for electron-microscopy imaging and spectroscopy, including instrument types such as SEM and TEM and multiple measurement modalities. However, its accelerator-oriented conceptual model and naming conventions may not fully represent all materials-microscopy concepts. The excerpt also highlights the value of a community-curated glossary as a machine- and human-readable semantic layer, independently of file format. More generally, the recommendations favor comprehensive, extensible metadata: bibliographic, sample, instrument-condition, and image-data information, with persistent sample identifiers and unlimited additional fields. contexts.context: The excerpt explains that scientific knowledge is lost when researchers move between projects, institutions, or careers because much of their expertise is context-dependent, undocumented, and difficult to transfer. Researchers may know not only standard procedures but also when and how to modify them for particular questions; this tacit knowledge can include practical skills, troubleshooting experience, software use, custom workflows, and the reasoning behind experimental choices. Departures to industry may further drain knowledge because proprietary techniques cannot be shared or academic contacts are lost. Short-term contracts, temporary positions, weak mentoring continuity, and pressure to publish can lead to abrupt departures without handover or documentation. For microscopy and other technically complex fields, preserving the rationale behind experimental decisions therefore requires more than storing final data or protocols: it requires recording adaptations, controls, validation, lessons learned, and contextual explanations. The article recommends dedicated time for documentation and knowledge transfer during transitions, comprehensive lab records, and platforms that capture both explicit and tacit expertise through annotated protocols, videos, interactive tutorials, community validation, and version control. These resources should preserve historical versions and evolve through collective review, helping future researchers understand not only what was done, but why particular approaches were selected.
contexts.question: How does science lose knowledge when researchers retire or move? What is the problem of tacit knowledge loss, knowledge drain, and preserving the rationale behind experimental decisions in microscopy?

contexts.context: The excerpt frames knowledge loss in microscopy as a problem of transferring both operational expertise and scientific judgment. Effective experiments depend on microscope-specific experience—knowing how to operate the instrument—as well as broad physical, chemical, or biological knowledge that determines what phenomena are worth investigating. Much of the rationale behind an experiment is embedded in decisions that may not be fully documented: selecting the object and region of interest, recognizing potentially significant morphology or spectra, choosing follow-up scans or spectroscopy, interpreting unexpected results, and deciding how to balance novelty against established hypotheses. When an experienced researcher retires or moves, this tacit knowledge can leave with them, creating a knowledge drain even if the instrument settings and raw data remain available. The distinction between automated and autonomous experiments reinforces the issue: automation may assist with low-latency tasks, but fully autonomous systems require explicit priors, historical knowledge, algorithmic biases, and experimental context. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies a major knowledge-preservation risk in microscopy: when the original data producer leaves, retires, or when data pass through multiple hands, essential metadata and contextual understanding can be lost. This is a form of knowledge drain that can make images, analyses, and experimental conclusions difficult to interpret, reproduce, validate, or reuse. The problem extends beyond missing technical fields: without documentation of the full workflow—from sample preparation and image acquisition through analysis and publication—future researchers may not know why particular experimental or processing decisions were made. Consequently, tacit knowledge held by the original researchers, such as assumptions, troubleshooting steps, parameter choices, and reasons for excluding or interpreting data, may disappear. The article stresses that accurate representation and reproducibility require complete documentation and structured data management from the beginning of a project. Core facilities can reduce this risk by supporting rigorous bioimaging research data management, using systems such as OMERO that preserve images, derived results, annotations, and links in structured formats. They can also help researchers meet evolving publication and sharing requirements, especially where guidelines are unfamiliar or lacking. Thus, preserving rationale requires proactive recording of metadata, methods, decisions, and data relationships rather than relying on researchers’ memories or later “data available on request” statements.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames knowledge loss in microscopy as the loss of experimental context, not merely the loss of raw images or spectra. Microscopy results depend on instrument configuration, probe condition, calibration, feedback settings, and acquisition history; much of this operational knowledge may reside with an experienced researcher and disappear when that person retires or moves. Conventional archives often fail to preserve unsaved tuning, failed attempts, probe and sample identities, environmental conditions, full time accounting, and—most importantly—the rationale for choosing one action over another. This creates a tacit-knowledge drain: successors may possess the data but lack the reasoning needed to interpret them, reproduce the work, diagnose failures, or understand how experimental decisions evolved. The proposed solution is to preserve longitudinal Instrument Traces, synchronized with Sample Traces and Decision Traces. These records would capture project, campaign, session, and event structure; instrument and controller states; actions, errors, recovery, environment, safety filtering, and decision provenance. Recording not only successful measurements but also exploratory paths and motivations could make expertise transferable, support operator training and replay, enable reproducible autonomy, and allow future researchers to analyze why an experiment proceeded as it did rather than seeing only its final data product.
contexts.question: How does science lose knowledge when researchers retire or move? What is the problem of tacit knowledge loss, knowledge drain, and preserving the rationale behind experimental decisions in microscopy?

Conferences, workshops, mentoring, and informal networking transmit techniques, experiences, and practical judgment; when participation is limited or community continuity is disrupted, this knowledge is less likely to transfer equitably and sustainably. answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We are preparing a proposal to the Microscopy Society of America (MSA) 2027 Strategic Initiatives program for an MSA-branded, open-source platform (CALIBER) that couples retrieval-augmented generation over the microscopy and microanalysis literature with a growing experimental dataset and an uncertainty-aware feedback loop to recommend high-fidelity SEM, EDS, EBSD, and XRF acquisition parameters for novel alloys, and that collects, preserves, and disseminates parameter-selection knowledge (technical procedures, underlying physics, and the rationale behind settings recommended in standards). Produce a citation-backed landscape review covering: (1) existing open-source software and data standards in microscopy/microanalysis relevant to this effort (e.g., HyperSpy, kikuchipy, pyxem, EMsoft, DREAM.3D, ImageJ/Fiji, napari, OME-Zarr, NeXus/FAIRmat) and what niches they do NOT cover; (2) existing repositories and resources for microscopy technical procedures and protocols (e.g., protocols.io, MyScope, DoITPoMS, nanoHUB, Microscopy Today and Microscopy & Microanalysis archives) and their gaps in capturing and preserving the rationale behind acquisition parameter choices; (3) evidence on FAIR-data and metadata-capture gaps in electron microscopy and microanalysis workflows; (4) precedents where scientific societies built branded open digital resources or tools, and what made them succeed or fail; (5) prior work on machine learning, literature mining, or autonomous/self-driving microscopy approaches to instrument parameter recommendation, and how an uncertainty-aware, literature-grounded recommender would differ; (6) successful models for involving students and early-career scientists in curating community scientific knowledge bases. Conclude with the strongest gap statements such a proposal could cite.

# Landscape Review for the CALIBER Proposal: Citation-Backed Gap Analysis for an MSA-Branded, Open-Source Microscopy Knowledge Platform

## 1. Open-Source Software and Data Standards in Microscopy/Microanalysis

The open-source microscopy ecosystem is rich in complementary tools for post-acquisition analysis, simulation, reconstruction, visualization, and data storage, yet no existing resource provides unified, literature-grounded acquisition-parameter recommendation.

**HyperSpy** serves as a foundational Python library for exploring, visualizing, and analyzing multidimensional microscopy and spectroscopy data, with lazy Dask-based processing that scales from desktops to high-performance computing (wei2022infrastructureforanalysis pages 1-3, pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 21-24). **Pyxem** and **py4DSTEM** extend this ecosystem for electron-diffraction and 4D-STEM analysis respectively (wei2022infrastructureforanalysis pages 1-3). **Kikuchipy** provides open-source EBSD pattern processing and indexing with interoperability to HyperSpy and EMsoft-generated simulated patterns. **EMsoft** is a physics-based forward-simulation suite for dynamical electron scattering and EBSD master-pattern generation; it is widely used for dictionary indexing and ML training but requires users to formulate candidate conditions rather than recommending them. **DREAM.3D** operates downstream of acquisition for 3D microstructure reconstruction, segmentation, and synthetic-volume generation. **Pycroscopy/pyUSID** provide a standardized USID/HDF5 data model linking source data, metadata, and derived results for improved traceability and reproducibility (somnath2019usidandpycroscopy pages 12-16, somnath2019usidandpycroscopy pages 19-23). **AtomAI** offers deep-learning analysis for microscopy images and spectra, including segmentation and structure–property mapping (pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 21-24). **ImageJ/Fiji** and **napari** serve as general-purpose image analysis and visualization platforms respectively.

For data standards, **OME-Zarr** provides cloud-native, chunked, multiscale array storage, but its semantics are predominantly oriented toward biological optical microscopy rather than materials microanalysis (taillon2025mardafairmaterials pages 3-4). **NeXus/FAIRmat NXem** offers a hierarchical, schema-validated representation of electron-microscopy experiments, covering instruments, samples, acquisition settings, and provenance for SEM, TEM, and STEM workflows (donni2025fairdatamanagementa pages 13-17, donni2025fairdatamanagement pages 13-17). However, even NXem has reported schema gaps for fields such as magnification, working distance, pixel size, and stage tilt in certain implementations (balestra2025fairdatamanagement pages 40-47).

**Critically, none of these tools provides a unified system that couples literature/standards retrieval with structured experimental data, multi-modal SEM/EDS/EBSD/XRF parameter recommendation, calibrated uncertainty, closed-loop learning, and preservation of procedural and decision rationale** (pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 5-7, pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 1-3, pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 3-5). The broader ecosystem remains fragmented, with limited benchmarks, integration strategies, and upstream experiment-planning capabilities (kuhbach2022communitydrivenmethodsfor pages 1-2, pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 5-7).

The following table summarizes the landscape and gaps:

| Tool / standard | Primary function | Key capabilities | Critical gaps relevant to CALIBER |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HyperSpy** | Analysis of multidimensional microscopy and spectroscopy data | Signal/data model; vendor-format import; decomposition, component analysis, visualization, lazy Dask-based processing; foundation for extensions including pyxem and kikuchipy. ## 2. Repositories for Microscopy Technical Procedures and Protocols

Existing protocol repositories and educational resources—including protocols.io, MyScope, DoITPoMS, nanoHUB, and the archives of *Microscopy Today* and *Microscopy & Microanalysis*—generally document the procedural steps of experiments but fail to systematically capture the expert reasoning behind parameter choices. Conventional publications compress acquisition, analysis, and post-processing information into short methods paragraphs, leaving inadequate space for the full chain of decisions needed to reproduce measurements (gammon2023anonlinerepository pages 1-2, gammon2023anonlinerepository pages 2-3). As Gammon et al. (2023) note, published settings are starting points that expert users must modify for their own instruments and specimens, yet the rationale for these modifications is rarely recorded (gammon2023anonlinerepository pages 2-3).

In electron microscopy specifically, effective experiments depend on both instrument-specific expertise and broader physical/chemical knowledge, including judgments about what is important to observe and what acquisition strategies to pursue (kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 4-7). Acquisition decisions are sequential: regions may be rescanned, spectroscopy may be initiated, or the sample may be modified based on morphology, spectral response, prior knowledge, or novelty. Repositories need to represent contextual priors, hypotheses, and the interaction between human decisions and ML/AI systems—not merely final parameters (kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 4-7). Current workflows are often custom, multistep processes refined through operator intuition over weeks, making expert knowledge extremely difficult to transfer or reproduce across laboratories (pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 3-5). The reasoning behind parameter choices remains implicit rather than systematically recorded, and repositories may document what settings were used without capturing why they were selected, what alternatives were considered, or how observations during an experiment changed subsequent decisions (pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 3-5, kuhbach2022communitydrivenmethodsfor pages 2-3).

## 3. FAIR-Data and Metadata-Capture Gaps in Electron Microscopy and Microanalysis

The materials microscopy community routinely fails to capture the complete experimental context needed to make data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. The MaRDA Working Group on FAIR Materials Microscopy Metadata recommends that instruments capture comprehensive metadata about operators, specimens/samples, instrument conditions, and data formation, and that microscopy data use standardized vocabularies and community-standard identifiers—recommendations that reflect the current inadequacy of practice (taillon2025mardafairmaterials pages 4-5, taillon2025mardafairmaterials pages 3-4). Commonly omitted metadata includes: unambiguous sample descriptions and persistent identifiers; microscope and detector identity; user identity; sample-preparation details; instrument settings and environmental conditions; deviations from standard procedures; and calibration procedures and results (taillon2025mardafairmaterials pages 4-5).

For SEM specifically, metadata at risk of being lost includes accelerating voltage, magnification, working distance, probe current, filament current, emitter type, detector information, microscope model and vendor, and control-software version—information that may be stored in proprietary structures (e.g., CZ_SEM EXIF tags) that are difficult to read automatically and are not guaranteed to survive format conversion (donni2025fairdatamanagementa pages 38-41, donni2025fairdatamanagement pages 38-41). Commercial instruments may produce proprietary formats, and vendor software can discard substantial portions of instrument-condition metadata when exporting because standard formats do not accommodate vendor- and instrument-specific fields (ghiringhelli2023sharedmetadatafor pages 13-14). The Shared Metadata for Data-Centric Materials Science initiative further highlights that experimental materials are often incompletely characterized and that environmental conditions such as temperature, air pressure, and humidity are commonly absent from records (ghiringhelli2023sharedmetadatafor pages 13-14).

A particularly significant finding is that FAIR metadata standards can structure and preserve acquisition context, but they do not by themselves capture the *causal rationale* for parameter selection—why a particular voltage was chosen, what the expected trade-offs were, or what standards clause justified the decision (donni2025fairdatamanagementa pages 13-17, donni2025fairdatamanagement pages 13-17). This represents a fundamental gap that CALIBER is designed to fill.

## 4. Precedents for Society-Branded Open Digital Resources

Multiple precedents inform how scientific societies and community organizations have successfully built branded open digital infrastructure. The **Computational Infrastructure for Geodynamics (CIG)** succeeded by combining a clear disciplinary mission with dissemination of open-source software, training, and enforceable practices such as open licenses, version control, and automated testing that eventually became community standards (katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 12-14). **NumFOCUS** built an effective umbrella model through fiscal sponsorship, educational programs, and support for widely used open-source projects. **rOpenSci** paired branded technical infrastructure—vetted, reusable R packages—with social infrastructure including peer review, communication channels, contributor support, and in-person events that built trust and sustained participation. **MolSSI** similarly combined software engineering, standards work, mentoring, and fellowships (katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 12-14).

In the life sciences, **ELIXIR** coordinates databases, software tools, training materials, and computational resources across an intergovernmental network, with 4OSS recommendations, benchmarking frameworks, and registries illustrating a branded ecosystem of open, discoverable, and reusable digital resources (katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 8-10). The **Science Gateways Community Institute (SGCI)** provides another model through catalogs, developer support, incubators, bootcamps, and student programs (katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 8-10). In scholarly publishing, **BioOne** created an open-access partnership among scientific societies, academic institutions, and the commercial sector supported by nearly 900 libraries (schweik2007freeopensourcesoftwareas pages 111-115), while the American Anthropological Association's **AnthroSource** portal was developed to provide members with broad online access while retaining society ownership and control of content (schweik2007freeopensourcesoftwareas pages 108-111).

**Key success factors** across these precedents include: community ownership and governance; concrete services that solve real needs; sustained maintenance and dedicated staff; training and capacity building; contributor recognition; integration with existing community activities rather than competing with them; and diversified financial support (katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 12-14, katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 14-16). **Failure risks** include volunteer commitments that exceed available capacity, initiatives that lack an established operational base, and attempts to launch entirely new activities without alignment to existing infrastructure. The WSSSPE experience illustrates this: working groups were more successful when aligned with existing activities, while attempts to create large independent programs generally failed (katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 12-14).

## 5. Machine Learning, Literature Mining, and Autonomous Microscopy Approaches

Substantial prior work exists on automated and autonomous experimentation in microscopy. Kalinin et al. (2021) provide a comprehensive framework distinguishing automated experiments—where AI performs rapid low-level analysis—from autonomous experimentation, where systems can seek additional information and adapt experimental progression (kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 7-10, kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 4-7). Key ML paradigms include **Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization** for recommending instrument parameters through acquisition functions that balance predicted performance and uncertainty; **reinforcement learning** for sequential instrument control; and **active learning** for targeting unusual or informative regions for additional measurements (kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 10-13, kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 22-25).

For SEM specifically, existing work has progressed from image-sharpness-based autofocus to deep-learning systems that evaluate focus quality and control working distance, beam-profile deconvolution methods that independently optimize focus and stigmator settings, and reinforcement learning for real-time imaging-parameter optimization (abbasgholinejadasbaghi2025metadatadrivenoptimizationin pages 12-15). A metadata-driven SEM optimization approach proposes automated recommendation of accelerating voltage, working distance, and aperture size using polynomial regression, metadata clustering, and iterative learning evaluated through no-reference image quality metrics (abbasgholinejadasbaghi2025metadatadrivenoptimizationin pages 10-12, abbasgholinejadasbaghi2025metadatadrivenoptimizationin pages 7-10).

**However, existing autonomous microscopy systems share critical limitations that CALIBER would address.** Current systems are primarily task-specific and data-driven: they identify predefined objects or regions (e.g., atoms, grain boundaries, domain walls) and trigger measurements according to fixed policies (pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 3-5). They do not synthesize domain literature and standards, they lack mechanisms for tracing recommendations to specific standards clauses or published evidence, and they do not learn from accumulating community experiments across heterogeneous instruments (pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 3-5, kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 18-22). An uncertainty-aware, literature-grounded recommender would differ by: explicitly encoding and exposing scientific priors and standards rationale; retrieving external knowledge during operation through RAG over the microscopy literature; quantifying and distinguishing aleatoric, epistemic, and out-of-distribution uncertainty; using that uncertainty to abstain or recommend informative follow-up measurements; detecting distribution shift across instruments and materials; and preserving human oversight and interpretability (kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 10-13, kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 7-10, kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 18-22). Kalinin et al. (2021) specifically identify the absence of a general framework balancing human and ML/AI decision-making with instrumental considerations as a key gap (kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 4-7).

## 6. Models for Involving Students and Early-Career Scientists

Multiple successful models demonstrate how trainees can contribute to community knowledge curation. **Software Carpentry** recruits researchers as volunteer peer instructors, trains them in evidence-based pedagogy, and enables them to teach reproducible workflows—creating a distributed model in which participants become both learners and contributors through collaborative lesson development, local Champions, and a Community Cookbook (katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 10-12). The broader Mozilla model similarly emphasizes cohort-based training, mentorship, mini-grants, and graduates returning as mentors (katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 10-12).

**Hackathons** provide focused collaborative events. The Mic-hackathon 2024 brought together ML experts and microscopy professionals to develop benchmark datasets, digital twins, and analysis tools for electron and scanning probe microscopy (pratiush2025michackathon2024hackathon pages 1-3). NASA's International Space Apps Challenge engaged more than 15,000 participants from 150 countries (ramachandran2021fromopendata pages 8-8). **Wiki-based curation** through PLOS Computational Biology's Topic Pages model allows students and early-career researchers to write peer-reviewed articles that are simultaneously published in the journal and on Wikipedia (arbuckle2021creatingopenscholarship pages 36-38, arbuckle2021creatingopenscholarship pages 33-36).

**Structured student projects** offer another model: Toelch and Ostwald (2018) describe MSc students converting existing datasets into the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS), reproducing analyses with readable code, and contributing to data-descriptor publications—developing data-management and reproducibility skills while producing reusable community resources (toelch2018digitalopenscience—teaching pages 5-6). Rainford et al. (2026) recommend targeted training programs, coding groups, peer-mentoring schemes, and AI-assisted documentation tools such as PRISM, where researchers record protocols hands-free and AI generates annotated video and text documentation (rainford2026knowledgepreservationin pages 6-7).

**Critical design principles** for sustained participation include: bounded, meaningful tasks with clear onboarding; structured mentorship and peer review; visible credit and recognition for contributions; version control so resources remain living records; accessible collaborative infrastructure; and a progression from participant to contributor to leader and community advocate (rainford2026knowledgepreservationin pages 6-7, katz2018communityorganizationschanging pages 10-12). One-off crowdsourcing without scaffolding or recognition is unlikely to maintain quality or participation (arbuckle2021creatingopenscholarship pages 38-41, arbuckle2021creatingopenscholarship pages 33-36).

### Overarching Gap Synthesis

Across all six domains, the evidence converges on a central finding: **the microscopy and microanalysis community possesses a maturing ecosystem of post-acquisition analysis tools and emerging metadata standards, but it lacks connective infrastructure that translates the community's accumulated literature, standards, and experimental experience into actionable, uncertainty-aware acquisition guidance while preserving the expert rationale that currently exists only as tacit knowledge** (kalinin2021automatedandautonomous pages 4-7, rainford2026knowledgepreservationin pages 2-3, rainford2026knowledgepreservationin pages 1-2).

Science loses knowledge when researchers retire or move between roles because much of the practical expertise behind experiments—troubleshooting experience, contextual understanding, and the reasoning behind methodological choices—is not captured in publications or records (rainford2026knowledgepreservationin pages 6-7, rainford2026knowledgepreservationin pages 2-3, rainford2026knowledgepreservationin pages 1-2). In microscopy specifically, preserving the rationale behind experimental decisions requires recording adaptations, controls, validation, lessons learned, and contextual explanations—not merely final data or protocols (rainford2026knowledgepreservationin pages 6-7, kalinin2608beyondfairdata pages 1-3). Kalinin et al. propose "Instrument Traces" that capture not only successful measurements but also exploratory paths, decision provenance, and motivations, making expertise transferable and supporting operator training and reproducible autonomy (kalinin2608beyondfairdata pages 1-3).

CALIBER would fill this gap by coupling retrieval-augmented generation over the microscopy literature with a growing experimental dataset and an uncertainty-aware feedback loop, creating a platform that not only recommends high-fidelity acquisition parameters but also collects, preserves, and disseminates the parameter-selection knowledge—technical procedures, underlying physics, and the rationale behind settings recommended in standards—that the community currently risks losing with each generation of retiring microscopists.

artifacts.artifact-00:
| Gap ID | Gap Domain | Gap Statement | Key Supporting References |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Software | Existing open microscopy packages provide strong capabilities for multidimensional analysis, diffraction simulation, microstructure reconstruction, visualization, and scalable storage, but they do not provide a unified, cross-modal recommender for selecting and justifying SEM, EDS, EBSD, and XRF acquisition parameters. | Wei et al. 2022; Somnath et al. 2019; Pratiush et al. 2025 (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003) |
| 2 | Software | The microscopy software ecosystem remains fragmented across post-acquisition analysis, simulation, storage, and instrument-specific control; standardized benchmarks, integration strategies, and transferable links between data, scientific objectives, and acquisition decisions remain underdeveloped. | Pratiush et al. 2025; Kühbach et al. 2022 (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000007) |
| 3 | Protocols | Conventional protocols and methods sections tend to preserve the procedural **what**, but not the expert **why**: alternatives considered, specimen- and instrument-specific constraints, expected trade-offs, parameter sensitivity, stopping criteria, or reasons for adapting settings during acquisition. | Kalinin et al. 2021; Gammon et al. 2023; Kühbach et al. 2022 (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) |
| 4 | Protocols | Microscopy workflows are often custom, multistep, and refined through local intuition over weeks; without structured decision histories, the rationale behind successful settings—and lessons from failed trials—cannot be readily transferred or compared across laboratories. | Pratiush et al. 2025; Rainford et al. 2026 (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000057) |
| 5 | FAIR Data | Materials microscopy routinely lacks complete, standardized experimental context, including persistent sample identity and history, preparation, operator and instrument identity, detector configuration, acquisition conditions, environmental state, calibrations, units, software versions, and deviations from standard procedures. | Taillon et al. 2025; Ghiringhelli et al. 2023 (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013) |
| 6 | FAIR Data | Proprietary formats and lossy exports can separate images, spectra, maps, or patterns from acquisition metadata; even emerging schemas may omit or inconsistently locate fields such as working distance, magnification, pixel size, stage tilt, and tilt compensation. | Donni 2025; Balestra 2025; Taillon et al. 2025 (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000046) |
| 7 | FAIR Data | NeXus/NXem and related standards can structure data, settings, provenance, and workflow context, but metadata representation alone does not capture the causal rationale for parameter selection, unsuccessful attempts, expert judgment, or evidence-backed recommendations. | Donni 2025; Taillon et al. 2025 (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049) |
| 8 | Society Platforms | Branded scientific digital resources succeed when a trusted organization supplies governance, maintenance, quality standards, training, contributor recognition, partnerships, and integration with established community activities; volunteer-only initiatives commonly stall when they exceed participants’ sustained capacity. | Katz et al. 2018; Schweik 2007 (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) |
| 9 | ML/Autonomous | Existing autonomous-microscopy work emphasizes task-specific tuning, fixed-policy target detection, Bayesian optimization, reinforcement learning, or adaptive sampling; it does not yet constitute a cross-technique recommender that grounds advice in traceable literature and standards while learning from accumulating community experiments. | Kalinin et al. 2021; Pratiush et al. 2025 (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000035) |
| 10 | Workforce | Community curation is sustainable when trainees receive bounded, meaningful tasks, structured onboarding, mentorship, review and version control, visible credit, and a progression from learner to contributor and mentor; one-off crowdsourcing without scaffolding or recognition is unlikely to maintain quality or participation. | Toelch & Ostwald 2018; Katz et al. 2018; Rainford et al. 2026 (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044) |


*Table: The strongest evidence-backed gaps across software, protocols, FAIR data, society platforms, autonomous microscopy, and workforce development. These statements position CALIBER as connective infrastructure rather than a replacement for existing analysis tools or data standards.*
artifacts.artifact-01:
| Tool / standard | Primary function | Key capabilities | Critical gaps relevant to CALIBER |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HyperSpy** | Analysis of multidimensional microscopy and spectroscopy data | Signal/data model; vendor-format import; decomposition, component analysis, visualization, lazy Dask-based processing; foundation for extensions including pyxem and kikuchipy. Can scale from desktops to HPC for large datasets (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000005) | Primarily post-acquisition analysis—not a literature-grounded planner for SEM/EDS/EBSD/XRF settings. Does not systematically preserve why settings were chosen, alternatives considered, failed trials, standards rationale, or uncertainty-calibrated recommendations (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000017) |
| **kikuchipy** | EBSD pattern processing and analysis | Open processing of electron-backscatter patterns; background correction, denoising, pattern handling, and indexing workflows; interoperates with HyperSpy-style multidimensional data and simulated patterns | Focuses on processing/indexing acquired EBSD patterns, not selecting accelerating voltage, beam current, working distance, detector geometry, exposure, gain, step size, or map strategy for a novel alloy. It does not retrieve standards/literature or preserve expert decision rationale |
| **pyxem** | Electron-diffraction and 4D-STEM analysis | Diffraction-data processing, virtual imaging, orientation/crystallographic analysis, and scalable lazy computation through the HyperSpy/Dask ecosystem (pqac-00000000) | Does not provide cross-modal SEM/EDS/EBSD/XRF acquisition planning, literature-grounded justification, standards-rationale capture, or an experimental feedback loop that learns calibrated recommendation uncertainty |
| **py4DSTEM** | Analysis of four-dimensional STEM datasets | Open-source calibration, diffraction analysis, property measurement, visualization, and HDF5-based data handling for large 4D-STEM datasets | Specialized for 4D-STEM analysis rather than SEM/EDS/EBSD/XRF parameter selection. Its data model does not itself encode the scientific rationale, rejected alternatives, standards interpretation, or uncertainty-aware recommendations needed by CALIBER |
| **EMsoft** | Physics-based electron-scattering, diffraction, imaging, and EBSD simulation | Dynamical forward simulation and master-pattern generation; supplies synthetic reference patterns for dictionary indexing, ML training, and validation | A forward-simulation suite, not a community recommender. Users must formulate candidate conditions; it does not synthesize literature and standards, learn from accumulating experiments, rank practical instrument settings with uncertainty, or retain operators’ decision histories |
| **DREAM.3D** | Three-dimensional microstructure reconstruction, characterization, and synthetic-volume generation | Pipeline-based segmentation and statistics; construction of representative volume elements; processing of EBSD-derived microstructures; integration with modeling and cloud workflows | Operates mainly downstream of acquisition. It does not recommend SEM, EDS, EBSD, or XRF acquisition conditions, connect recommendations to cited physics/standards, or curate the rationale behind instrument settings |
| **pycroscopy / pyUSID** | Standardized storage, provenance, and analysis of imaging and spectroscopic data | USID/HDF5 data model; translators; scalable analysis; links source data, metadata, and derived results to improve traceability and reproducibility (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006) | Captures data and processing provenance better than most analysis packages, but not the complete upstream decision trace: why an acquisition was configured a certain way, what alternatives failed, or how literature and standards justify a recommendation. Cross-file provenance was also identified as incomplete (pqac-00000001) |
| **AtomAI** | Deep-learning analysis of microscopy images and spectra | Segmentation, atomic-coordinate extraction, invariant representation learning, image–spectrum relationships, and links to first-principles modeling | Primarily interprets acquired data. It is not a validated, cross-instrument acquisition recommender and does not inherently retrieve source literature, expose standards-based rationales, capture procedural knowledge, or distinguish aleatoric, epistemic, and out-of-distribution uncertainty (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000033) |
| **ImageJ / Fiji** | General-purpose image processing and scientific-image analysis | Mature GUI; extensive plugin and macro ecosystem; segmentation, measurement, filtering, registration, and reproducible scripted workflows across many image types | Broad image analysis but limited native representation of materials-microscopy acquisition context. It does not recommend SEM/EDS/EBSD/XRF settings or preserve literature evidence, standards rationale, adaptive decision histories, and calibrated confidence |
| **napari** | Interactive, extensible visualization of multidimensional images | Python-based n-dimensional viewer; layers, annotations, plugins, and interactive integration with analysis and ML workflows | A visualization and plugin host rather than an acquisition-knowledge system. Any recommendation, literature retrieval, metadata validation, rationale capture, or uncertainty feedback must be supplied by external plugins and infrastructure |
| **OME-Zarr** | Cloud-native storage and exchange of large multidimensional bioimaging data | Chunked, compressed, multiscale arrays; parallel and remote access; interoperable visualization and analysis; OME-associated image metadata | Strong for scalable pixel/array transport, but OME semantics are predominantly oriented toward biological optical microscopy rather than materials microanalysis (pqac-00000047). It neither recommends parameters nor natively represents the reasoning, physics, standards clauses, failed settings, and uncertainty behind SEM/EDS/EBSD/XRF choices |
| **NeXus / FAIRmat NXem** | Hierarchical, schema-validated representation of electron-microscopy data and metadata | NXem can organize experiments, instruments, samples, hardware, beam generation, images, spectra, acquisition settings, time-dependent metadata, and provenance for SEM/TEM/STEM workflows (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000049) | Provides a promising storage target, not a recommender or knowledge base. It does not itself infer settings or capture tacit rationale. Coverage and terminology remain incomplete for some materials-microscopy uses; reported schema gaps include fields such as magnification, working distance, pixel size, stage tilt, and tilt compensation in particular implementations (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048) |
| **Collective landscape** | Complementary ecosystem spanning simulation, acquisition-data representation, analysis, reconstruction, ML, and visualization | Existing projects supply many components CALIBER should reuse rather than duplicate: scalable arrays, translators, schemas, provenance, domain algorithms, forward models, viewers, and plugin systems | No listed resource unifies **literature/standards retrieval + structured experimental data + multi-modal SEM/EDS/EBSD/XRF parameter recommendation + calibrated uncertainty/abstention + closed-loop learning + preservation of procedural and decision rationale**. The broader ecosystem remains fragmented, with limited benchmarks, integration strategies, instrument APIs, and upstream experiment planning (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000020) |


*Table: This table maps major open-source microscopy tools and data standards to their established niches and identifies the acquisition-recommendation and knowledge-preservation functions that remain uncovered. It shows that CALIBER would integrate and extend—not duplicate—the existing ecosystem.*

info.query: We are preparing a proposal to the Microscopy Society of America (MSA) 2027 Strategic Initiatives program for an MSA-branded, open-source platform (CALIBER) that couples retrieval-augmented generation over the microscopy and microanalysis literature with a growing experimental dataset and an uncertainty-aware feedback loop to recommend high-fidelity SEM, EDS, EBSD, and XRF acquisition parameters for novel alloys, and that collects, preserves, and disseminates parameter-selection knowledge (technical procedures, underlying physics, and the rationale behind settings recommended in standards). Produce a citation-backed landscape review covering: (1) existing open-source software and data standards in microscopy/microanalysis relevant to this effort (e.g., HyperSpy, kikuchipy, pyxem, EMsoft, DREAM.3D, ImageJ/Fiji, napari, OME-Zarr, NeXus/FAIRmat) and what niches they do NOT cover; (2) existing repositories and resources for microscopy technical procedures and protocols (e.g., protocols.io, MyScope, DoITPoMS, nanoHUB, Microscopy Today and Microscopy & Microanalysis archives) and their gaps in capturing and preserving the rationale behind acquisition parameter choices; (3) evidence on FAIR-data and metadata-capture gaps in electron microscopy and microanalysis workflows; (4) precedents where scientific societies built branded open digital resources or tools, and what made them succeed or fail; (5) prior work on machine learning, literature mining, or autonomous/self-driving microscopy approaches to instrument parameter recommendation, and how an uncertainty-aware, literature-grounded recommender would differ; (6) successful models for involving students and early-career scientists in curating community scientific knowledge bases. Conclude with the strongest gap statements such a proposal could cite.
